what-is-pfp.body:
Peripheral facial paralysis means the seventh cranial nerve — the facial nerve — has stopped carrying signals properly to the muscles on one side of your face. The muscles themselves are usually fine. They are simply not receiving instructions.

The nerve involved

The facial nerve leaves the brainstem, travels through a narrow bony canal in the skull, and fans out across the face. It controls almost every expression you make, and it also carries fibres for tear production, some saliva glands, taste on part of the tongue, and a small muscle that dampens loud sound in the middle ear.

That branching explains why facial paralysis rarely presents as movement loss alone. A dry or watering eye, altered taste, or sound feeling uncomfortably loud on one side are all consistent with the same single nerve being affected.

The narrow bony canal matters too. When the nerve becomes inflamed anywhere along that stretch, it has almost nowhere to swell into. The pressure itself contributes to the loss of function, which is part of why anti-inflammatory treatment given early can change the course.

Why it happens

In roughly seven out of ten cases no specific cause is identified, and the diagnosis is Bell's palsy — an idiopathic facial palsy, most likely driven by inflammation and swelling of the nerve, with reactivated herpes simplex virus the leading suspect in much of the research.

The remaining cases have identifiable causes: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (varicella zoster, typically with a painful rash and often a slower recovery), Lyme disease in endemic regions, middle ear infection, trauma or fracture, surgery near the nerve, tumours pressing on its path, and rarer neurological and autoimmune conditions.

The distinction matters because the cause shapes both treatment and expected timeline. If nobody has established which of these applies to you, that is a conversation to have with your doctor rather than with an app.

What it is not

Facial paralysis is not a stroke, though the fear is entirely understandable and the two get confused constantly. The distinguishing pattern is the forehead. In peripheral facial paralysis the whole side of the face is affected, including the forehead and the eye. In a stroke the forehead is usually spared because it receives nerve supply from both sides of the brain.

Even so: sudden facial weakness accompanied by arm weakness, confusion, difficulty speaking, or a severe headache is an emergency. Call emergency services. It is far better to be assessed and sent home than to reason your way through a stroke at home.

It is also not caused by cold air, draughts, or sitting near a window — a persistent folk belief with no supporting evidence. And it is not something you caused through stress or by neglecting yourself.

How doctors grade it

Most clinicians use the House-Brackmann scale, which runs from I (normal) to VI (complete paralysis, no movement at all). Some use the more detailed Sunnybrook system, which scores resting symmetry, voluntary movement, and synkinesis separately.

These grades are useful shorthand between clinicians. They are less useful as something to carry around as an identity. A grade is a snapshot of one moment, and it moves.

What recovery usually looks like

For Bell's palsy specifically, the published figures are broadly encouraging. Most people show the first signs of recovery within three weeks. A large majority recover completely or near-completely. A minority — often cited around 15–20% — retain some lasting asymmetry, weakness, or synkinesis.

Recovery is not linear. Plateaus of several weeks are common and are not a sign that something has gone wrong. Progress also tends to arrive region by region rather than all at once: the mouth commonly returns before the eye, and the forehead is often last.

What none of this tells you is what will happen to you. Population statistics describe groups. We will not offer you a prediction, because an honest one is not available.

stages-of-recovery.body:
Rehabilitation for facial paralysis is not one programme done for longer. What helps in week two can actively hold you back in month four, and the reverse is also true. So the work is organised into five stages defined by what the nerve and muscle are actually doing, not by how many days have passed.

Why stages rather than weeks

Two people with the same diagnosis on the same date can be in genuinely different places six weeks later. Time since onset is a useful filter, but the deciding factor is function: is there voluntary movement, is it isolated, is there tightness, is there synkinesis. Your stage is set from your assessment answers and adjusted from your scans and your clinician's input.

Stage 1 — Protect

The nerve is inflamed and not conducting well. No amount of muscle work changes that, and effortful work risks establishing patterns you will spend months unpicking.

So the programme is deliberately quiet. Protect the eye, keep tissue supple with light massage, support the resting position of the face with light taping, and rest. This stage frustrates people who want to be doing something. The something is protection.

Stage 2 — Activate

A flicker appears. It may be visible only to you, only in a mirror, only in one region. That is enough to work with.

The goal is to find the smallest movement you can reliably produce and repeat it accurately. Not the largest. Effortful straining pulls in neighbouring muscles and the opposite side of the face, and the nervous system learns whatever it repeats — including the compensations. Small and correct beats large and recruited, every time.

Stage 3 — Coordination

Movement is present but it does not go only where you send it. The eye narrows when you smile. The mouth corner twitches when you close the eye. This is synkinesis, and it happens because regenerating nerve fibres do not all find their original destinations.

Coordination work teaches separation: small movements, held slowly, with the linked region consciously kept still. It is the least satisfying stage — the numbers move slowly and it demands attention — and it is where the difference between a good long-term outcome and a mediocre one is usually made.

Stage 4 — Refine

The face works. The work shifts from producing movement to controlling it at the effort levels real life uses: speaking, eating, expressions in conversation. Tension management matters as much as activation now, because tightness quietly limits range even when strength has returned.

Stage 5 — Maintain

Recovery flattens. It does not usually reverse, but range can be lost quietly if everything stops. A shorter maintenance routine plus periodic scans keeps drift visible.

Moving between stages

Stage changes come from three places: your scan data, your own reports of what you can do, and your clinician. You will always be told why a stage changed and what specifically changes in your programme as a result.

Stages can also move backwards — after illness, a period of high fatigue, or a stretch of high tension. That is a normal adjustment of the programme to the face you have this month, not a failure and not lost ground.

facial-taping-guide.body:
Elastic therapeutic tape applied to the face has three plausible mechanisms: mechanical support against gravity, sensory input that helps the brain locate a region it has partly lost track of, and a directional cue that makes a correct movement easier to find. The evidence base is modest and mostly small studies. We are telling you that up front.

What taping does

In practice, patients most consistently report three things: the resting position of the face is better while the tape is on, movements feel like they take less effort, and the affected side feels more present. That last one sounds vague and turns out to matter — you cannot easily move a region you have stopped sensing.

What taping does not do

Tape does not speed up nerve regeneration. It does not replace exercises. It does not work better with more tension — the opposite, reliably. And it is not a substitute for eye protection: never tape across the eyelid as a way of closing the eye unless a clinician has specifically shown you a technique for it.

Before you start

  • Patch test first. Apply a 3 cm piece to your inner forearm for 24 hours before you put anything on your face.
  • Clean, dry, oil-free skin. No moisturiser, no make-up, no sunscreen underneath. Tape will not hold, and it will drag when it lifts.
  • Round every corner. Square corners catch on pillows and clothing and lift within the hour.
  • Cut what you need before you start. Handling adhesive with one hand while holding a mirror does not go well.

Applying tape

The pattern is the same for every strip: anchor, stretch, anchor. Lay the first two centimetres down with no stretch at all. Apply the middle section with the intended stretch. Lay the last two centimetres with no stretch. Then rub the whole strip firmly for ten seconds — the adhesive is heat-activated and it will not bond otherwise.

Apply with the face at rest, not mid-smile. Tape applied on a stretched face pulls constantly once the face relaxes.

Tension

This is the single most common mistake, and it is always in the same direction: too much.

The check is physical, not visual. You should be able to slide a fingertip under the middle of the strip. If the skin is puckered, blanched, or visibly dragged, the tension is wrong. If the tape is pulling your eye or your lip out of a natural position, remove it and start again.

Your stage sets the target: resting support is very light, movement assist is moderate, directional guides are light again. Your programme tells you which one you are on today.

Removing tape

Slowly, in the direction of hair growth, pressing the skin down just behind the tape as you peel. In the shower is easiest — warm water loosens the adhesive. Never rip it off. Facial skin is thin, and a tear takes you off tape for a week.

When to stop

Remove the tape and do not reapply if you get itching, burning, redness that persists after removal, a rash, blistering, or any broken skin. Contact your clinician if a skin reaction does not settle within a day, and take a scheduled rest day from tape at least weekly regardless.

facial-exercises-guide.body:
Facial neuromuscular retraining is not strength training. That single sentence explains most of what follows, and unlearning the gym instinct is the hardest part of the programme for most people.

The core principle

The nervous system learns what it repeats. If you produce a smile with effort and your eye narrows as part of it, you have practised a smile-with-eye-narrowing. Twenty repetitions of that make the linkage stronger, not weaker.

So the target is always the largest movement you can make cleanly, and no larger. If the clean version is tiny, the clean version is the exercise.

Effort level

Roughly a third of your maximum. If you are gritting your teeth, tensing your neck, or holding your breath, you are far past it.

This feels wrong. It feels like not really trying. It is the correct dose.

Keeping the good side quiet

The unaffected side will try to do the work. It is stronger, its pathway is intact, and it responds faster. Left alone, it takes over and the asymmetry you are working on gets worse during the exercise.

The fix is physical: hold the unaffected side still with two fingers. For the brow, hold the good eyebrow down. For the mouth, rest a fingertip lightly at the strong corner. It looks awkward and it works.

Using a mirror

A mirror gives you the visual feedback the nerve currently is not providing, and in early stages it is close to essential. Sit square to it, at eye level, in even light — light from one side creates shadow asymmetry that will make you chase a problem that is not there.

Later in recovery, deliberately spend part of each session without the mirror. Real life does not come with one, and movements that only work under observation are not finished.

How much is enough

Short and frequent beats long and occasional. Two sessions of twelve to fifteen minutes will do more than one session of forty, because quality collapses with facial fatigue and you cannot feel it happening reliably.

Signs you have done enough for now: the movement is getting smaller rather than larger, the linked movement is getting more obvious, twitching increases, or the area feels heavy or achy. Stop. Coming back tomorrow is not a compromise.

The five common mistakes

  1. Too much effort. The most common, by a wide margin, and the most costly.
  2. Too many repetitions. Everything after fatigue trains the compensation.
  3. Ignoring the good side. It takes over silently.
  4. Chewing gum as exercise. Trains the wrong muscles and reliably increases tightness and synkinesis. Please do not.
  5. Skipping release work. Once tightness appears, it limits range more than weakness does. Stretching is not the optional part.

daily-routine.body:
The exercises are perhaps a quarter of what makes recovery go well. The rest is the ordinary daily management that protects the eye, keeps you eating and sleeping, and keeps the programme survivable across months rather than days.

Eye care comes first

If your eye does not close fully, this is the most important paragraph on this page. The cornea is protected by the blink, and without a complete blink it dries out. Corneal damage from exposure is the one complication of facial paralysis that can cause permanent harm to something other than movement, and it is largely preventable.

Preservative-free lubricating drops during the day, roughly every two to three hours. Ointment at night, with the lid taped closed or a moisture chamber if your clinician has advised it. Sunglasses outdoors, wind and dust included. And see a doctor the same day if the eye becomes painful or red, or your vision changes.

Eating and drinking

Food collecting in the affected cheek, drinks escaping the lip seal, biting the inside of the cheek without feeling it. These are mechanical problems with mechanical answers: smaller mouthfuls, slower pace, food placed towards the stronger side, and a rinse and mirror check after meals.

Eating alone for a while, if that is what makes meals bearable, is a reasonable choice and not a failure of resilience.

Fatigue is real

Facial fatigue is under-recognised and patients consistently report it as one of the hardest parts. Holding an expression, or holding a face still, takes effort that used to be free. Concentrating on a conversation while managing your face is genuinely tiring.

Practise when you are freshest, usually the morning. Expect movement quality to be worse in the evening — that is fatigue, not decline.

Sleep

On your back, or on the unaffected side. Face-down pressure on the affected side for eight hours works against everything you did during the day. Eye protection goes on before lights out, not after you are already half asleep.

Anchoring the routine

Attach sessions to things you already do without deciding — after brushing your teeth, after the morning coffee, before your evening shower. Habits attached to existing habits survive. Habits attached to intentions do not.

Keep the tape, the drops, and the mirror in one place. Friction is what actually ends programmes, not motivation.

Missed days

You will miss days. A missed day costs you that day and nothing more — there is no compounding penalty, and doubling up tomorrow is worse than a normal session, because fatigue degrades quality.

Open the app, do today's session, carry on. The record is there so you and your clinician can see patterns, not so anyone can grade you.

research-evidence.body:
We would rather tell you where the evidence is thin than imply it is strong everywhere. This page is updated when the picture changes.

How to read this page

Not all evidence is equal. Systematic reviews of randomised trials sit at the top; small single-centre studies and clinical consensus sit lower. Facial rehabilitation has relatively few large trials, partly because blinding a physical therapy intervention is difficult and partly because most patients with Bell's palsy recover well regardless, which makes treatment effects hard to isolate.

Corticosteroids

Well supported. Systematic review evidence supports early oral corticosteroids for Bell's palsy, ideally started within 72 hours of onset. This is a medical decision made by your doctor, not something an app manages.

Antivirals

Mixed. Antivirals alone do not show clear benefit for Bell's palsy. Combined with steroids they may add a small benefit in severe cases; guidelines differ. For Ramsay Hunt syndrome, where zoster is the established cause, antiviral treatment is standard.

Facial retraining

Moderately supported, strongest for synkinesis. Reviews of physical therapy for facial palsy find that tailored neuromuscular retraining improves outcomes, with the clearest signal in chronic cases and synkinesis. Two consistent findings shape our programme: individualised beats generic, and low-effort accurate work beats forceful repetition.

Taping

Limited but positive. Small studies report improved resting symmetry and reduced perceived effort. Sample sizes are small, blinding is essentially impossible, and long-term effects are not established. We include taping because the reported benefit is consistent and the risk is low, not because the evidence is strong.

Electrical stimulation

Not recommended in acute recovery. Evidence is inconsistent and there is a theoretical concern that stimulation during reinnervation may worsen synkinesis. We do not include it. If a clinician has prescribed it for you specifically, follow their advice over ours.

Our own data

Our symmetry score is a geometric measurement derived from facial landmarks: distances and angles on the affected side are compared with the mirrored unaffected side, normalised against your own baseline. It is not a House-Brackmann or Sunnybrook grade and does not translate to one.

Repeat-scan testing under varied lighting and head position gives a typical measurement variability of about ±2.5 points, which is why we show an uncertainty range and treat changes under roughly 3 points as noise rather than progress.

Aggregate outcome figures from our own users are observational: people who choose a structured programme and stay with it differ systematically from those who do not. We report those numbers as what our users experienced, never as proof of what the programme caused.

What we do not know

  • The optimal daily dose of facial exercise. Current guidance is reasoned, not established by dose-response trials.
  • Whether taping changes long-term outcomes as opposed to short-term comfort and symmetry.
  • Which patients benefit most from which specific exercise, beyond broad stage-matching.
  • How our symmetry score relates to what patients actually care about — eating, speaking, being understood.
